hints: Start by recalling what each method actually does to DNA - one adds a whole new foreign gene carried on a vector, the other makes a precise change to a gene already present.
Think about the end result for the organism - if you add a foreign gene or if you edit an existing gene, will the characteristics change in both cases?
Consider enzymes - both methods need to cut DNA at some point, but what cuts plasmid DNA in the old method and what cuts chromosomal DNA in the new method?
Focus on the word delete - removing a section of the organism's own DNA is different from inserting extra DNA from another species.
Remember how CRISPR finds its target - what type of nucleic acid is complementary to the target DNA sequence and guides the cutting enzyme to the exact place?
walkthrough:
What the old plasmid method does**
Think of the 1973 method as add-a-gene. A restriction endonuclease cuts open the plasmid vector and the donor DNA, ligase joins them to make recombinant DNA, and the plasmid carries the foreign gene into the host. Because foreign DNA from another species is added, the host becomes transgenic and its characteristics are modified.

What the new gene editing method does**
Think of gene editing as edit-your-own-gene. It can also add DNA to make a transgenic organism and so modify characteristics, but it can also change or delete part of the organism's own DNA without necessarily adding foreign DNA. That is why delete unwanted DNA applies only to gene editing.

Enzymes and targeting**
Both methods use an enzyme that cuts DNA. The old method uses restriction endonucleases to cut plasmid and donor DNA. The new method uses a nuclease such as Cas9 to cut the target chromosomal DNA. Only gene editing uses a guide RNA molecule that is complementary to the target gene to locate it precisely by base pairing.

Final answer: genetic engineering using a plasmid: tick for produce transgenic organism, modify characteristics, uses enzyme that cuts DNA. gene editing: tick for all five statements. Only gene editing ticks for delete unwanted DNA and use RNA to precisely locate target gene.

hints: Look at Fig. 4.1 - wild type leaves are not resistant, so which bar shows the largest area of leaf with canker disease in $mm^2$?
walkthrough:
Link resistance to the bar height**
Wild type means not gene edited, so it has no added resistance to citrus canker bacteria. After exposure it will develop the most disease. In Fig. 4.1 bar A is about $2.2 mm^2$, much higher than B at about $0.44 mm^2$ and C at about $0.18 mm^2$, so A must be the wild type.
Final answer: A - has largest area of leaf with canker disease (about $2.2 mm^2$).

hints: Start from the biology in Fig. 4.1 - if edited leaves have almost no canker, what does that mean for healthy functional leaf area, photosynthesis and fruit production?
Now think like a farmer and then like a shopper - what happens to farmer income and to price and quality of oranges if yield is higher and more reliable?
Think about how canker is normally controlled - if trees are already resistant, what costly and polluting sprays are no longer needed?
walkthrough:
More healthy leaf means more food**
Canker reduces functional leaf area, so less photosynthesis and less growth and fruit. Gene edited trees B and C show strong resistance, so they keep healthy leaves, maintain photosynthesis and produce higher yield of oranges. That helps food supply.

Better livelihoods and cheaper quality food**
Higher, more reliable yield gives growers more fruit to sell and more income. For society this means greater availability of good quality oranges at lower cost to the consumer.

Less chemical control**
Resistant trees do not need repeated spraying with bactericidal chemicals. That saves money for farmers and reduces chemical exposure and environmental pollution for the community.

Final answer: Any three from: increased yield / more food to help meet global demand; improved quality of fruit / crop; more income for farmers / growers; cheaper fruit for consumers; reduced use of bactericidal chemicals / pesticides.
